messages.content:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Oil (lamp oil)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the divine presence, empowering, and anointing that sustains the believer's spiritual light. This reading is applied especially to the parable of the ten virgins, where possessing oil is taken to mean having the indwelling Spirit (or the genuine spiritual life the Spirit produces), which cannot be borrowed from another person.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13 (parable of the ten virgins; the wise have oil, the foolish do not)",
    "Zechariah 4:1-6 (lampstand fed by oil; 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit')",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 (pure olive oil to keep the tabernacle lamp burning continually)",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 (anointing with oil accompanied by the Spirit coming upon David)",
    "Isaiah 61:1 / Luke 4:18 (anointing linked to the Spirit of the Lord)",
    "Acts 10:38 (God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power)",
    "1 John 2:20, 27 (the 'anointing' from the Holy One that abides in believers)",
    "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('oil of gladness' associated with divine anointing)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Spiritual preparedness/readiness or perseverance for Christ's return — the oil simply represents being ready, without a specific allegorical referent; many modern academic commentators argue the parable's point is watchfulness and warn against pressing the oil for a precise symbol.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:13 ('Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour')",
        "Matthew 24:42-44 (context of readiness discourse)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works or deeds of love/charity — an interpretation with deep patristic roots (e.g., readings associated with Augustine and other Fathers, echoed in some Catholic and Orthodox teaching), where the oil is works of mercy that keep the lamp of profession burning.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:14-16 (let your light shine through good works)",
        "Matthew 25:31-46 (immediately following context of deeds of mercy)",
        "James 2:14-26 (faith without works is dead)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Grace — divine grace received and maintained in the soul, a reading found in Catholic and Orthodox spiritual writing (e.g., Seraphim of Sarov's teaching on acquiring the Holy Spirit blends this with the Spirit reading).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13",
        "Zechariah 4:1-6"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Genuine saving faith or authentic inner spiritual life distinguishing true believers from nominal ones — the oil marks the reality behind an outward profession.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (both groups look alike outwardly; only the oil distinguishes them)",
        "Matthew 7:21-23 ('I never knew you')"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Word of God or joy/gladness (oil of gladness) sustaining the believer's light.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 119:105 (word as lamp)",
        "Psalm 45:7 (oil of gladness)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a recognizable popular-level consensus, strongest in evangelical, Pentecostal, and charismatic teaching, that lamp oil symbolizes the Holy Spirit, grounded in the biblical association of oil with anointing and the Spirit (1 Sam 16:13; Zech 4; Acts 10:38; 1 John 2:20-27). However, this consensus is stratified: critical and academic commentators on Matthew 25 frequently resist assigning the oil any single allegorical meaning, treating it as a narrative device signifying readiness, while the patristic and Catholic tradition often reads it as good works or charity. So the 'Holy Spirit' reading is dominant in devotional and popular teaching but is contested or bracketed in scholarly exegesis. Note also that oil more broadly (anointing oil, oil for healing, e.g., James 5:14; Mark 6:13) reinforces the Spirit association, but the question here concerns lamp oil specifically."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "The Holy Spirit—especially the Spirit’s indwelling presence, sustaining grace, and power that enables believers to remain spiritually awake and bear light—is the symbolic meaning most commonly assigned to lamp oil in popular Christian teaching.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1–13: the wise virgins possess sufficient oil for their lamps and are ready when the bridegroom arrives; this is frequently interpreted as possessing the Spirit or an inward spiritual life that cannot be borrowed at the last moment.",
    "Zechariah 4:1–14, especially 4:6: the lampstand supplied with oil is associated with the declaration, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”",
    "1 Samuel 16:13: David is anointed with oil, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, supporting the broader Christian association between oil and the Holy Spirit.",
    "Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18: anointing and the Spirit are closely linked in messianic language.",
    "Acts 10:38: God anoints Jesus “with the Holy Spirit and with power.”",
    "Exodus 27:20–21 and Leviticus 24:1–4: pure oil continually sustains the sanctuary lamps, contributing typologically to the ideas of enduring divine presence and spiritual light."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Readiness, vigilance, perseverance, or faithful preparation for Christ’s coming, without assigning the oil a separate symbolic referent.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13 explicitly concludes, “Keep awake,” making readiness the parable’s direct emphasis.",
        "Many historical-critical and literary interpreters caution against decoding every element of a parable; on this reading, the oil functions narratively as what distinguishes those prepared for delay from those unprepared."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Saving faith, genuine discipleship, inward spiritual life, or personal relationship with Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13 portrays an inwardly possessed and nontransferable preparedness that must exist before the bridegroom arrives.",
        "Matthew 7:21–23 and 25:10–12 are sometimes connected through the language of being known or excluded, leading interpreters to emphasize authentic discipleship rather than the Spirit specifically."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works, obedience, love, or charity manifested through the believer’s light.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:14–16 identifies disciples as lights and connects shining light with good works.",
        "Historical Christian interpretation has sometimes understood the oil of Matthew 25 as charity or virtuous deeds that sustain the lamp of profession."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Scripture, divine truth, or the word of God that nourishes spiritual illumination.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 119:105 calls God’s word a lamp and a light.",
        "Proverbs 6:23 similarly associates the commandment and teaching with lamp and light, though neither passage directly identifies oil with the word."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The general grace, blessing, healing, consecration, joy, or abundance of God rather than specifically the Holy Spirit.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 23:5 and 45:7 use oil in contexts of blessing, honor, and joy.",
        "Isaiah 61:3 speaks of the “oil of gladness.”",
        "Mark 6:13 and James 5:14 associate oil with healing.",
        "Exodus 30:22–33 uses sacred anointing oil for consecration."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Oil broadly has several biblical functions, so there is no single settled symbolic meaning applicable in every context. The Holy Spirit is the most recognizable Christian symbolic association, particularly in typological and devotional teaching. For the lamp oil in Matthew 25 specifically, many interpreters regard readiness for the bridegroom—not a precise identification of the oil—as the safest and most textually explicit interpretation."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "the Holy Spirit (as empowering presence, anointing, and fuel for spiritual light/witness)",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13",
    "Zechariah 4:1-14",
    "Exodus 27:20-21",
    "Leviticus 24:1-4",
    "1 Samuel 16:13",
    "Isaiah 61:1",
    "Acts 10:38",
    "1 John 2:20, 27"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "spiritual preparedness, readiness, or vigilance for Christ's return",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "faith, grace, or an enduring personal relationship with God",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "good works, righteous deeds, or practical charity that sustains witness",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "joy, gladness, or healing/consolation (broader oil symbolism occasionally applied)",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 45:7",
        "Hebrews 1:9",
        "James 5:14",
        "Isaiah 61:3"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Across historic and modern Christian interpretation, oil (including lamp oil) is most consistently linked to the Holy Spirit; the Parable of the Ten Virgins supplies the main lamp-oil context and generates secondary readings of readiness/faith/works, yet these are typically understood as effects or evidences of the Spirit rather than replacements for that primary symbolism. No major tradition rejects the Spirit association for oil in general."
}

BOOK ENTRY
Spirit-taught truth and correction received, kept, and worked into proven obedience — the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored inwardly; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ex 25:6; 27:20; Ps 141:5; Prov 21:20; 23:23; 27:5-9; Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6-14; Matt 25:3-9; 5:16) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20, and The Anointing

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Exodus 25:6 — Oil for the light, spices for anointing oil, and for sweet incense,
Exodus 27:20 — And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always.
Psalms 141:5 — Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.
Proverbs 21:20 — There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
Proverbs 23:23 — Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.
Proverbs 27:5 — Open rebuke is better than secret love.
Proverbs 27:6 — Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Proverbs 27:7 — The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.
Proverbs 27:8 — As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place.
Proverbs 27:9 — Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
Ezekiel 36:27 — And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
Zechariah 4:6 — Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Zechariah 4:7 — Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it.
Zechariah 4:8 — Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,
Zechariah 4:9 — The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you.
Zechariah 4:10 — For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Zechariah 4:11 — Then answered I, and said unto him, What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick and upon the left side thereof?
Zechariah 4:12 — And I answered again, and said unto him, What be these two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden oil out of themselves?
Zechariah 4:13 — And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord.
Zechariah 4:14 — Then said he, These are the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth.
Matthew 25:3 — They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them:
Matthew 25:4 — But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Matthew 25:5 — While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.
Matthew 25:6 — And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.
Matthew 25:7 — Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
Matthew 25:8 — And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
Matthew 25:9 — But the wise answered, saying, Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.
Matthew 5:16 — Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

- MATCH: substantially the same meaning as the recognizable consensus.
- REFINED: compatible with the consensus but materially sharper, narrower,
  broader, or more precisely supported.
- DIVERGENT: contradicts or displaces a recognizable common interpretation.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus covers the book's central claim; the book
  stakes a meaning not represented by the blind responses.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
